content_metadata.description: This educational video explores the uses and properties of different metals such as gold, silver, copper, aluminum, and steel. It explains their reactivity, benefits, and how they have historically impacted human society, especially in construction and industry.

qAndA.question: What graphic is used to represent the subject of Chemistry in the introductory animation?

qAndA.answer: Because they are unreactive, and will stay shiny and untarnished
qAndA.question: Why are gold and silver often used in jewelry given as gifts?

qAndA.answer: It is too expensive, plastic piping is much cheaper
qAndA.question: Why does copper no longer get used for water pipes?

qAndA.answer: It is less dense than most metals, making it lightweight. Additionally, it can be made into a strong alloy.
qAndA.question: Why is aluminum a good choice for building aircraft?

qAndA.answer: Steel is considerably stronger than iron and cheap to make, which has allowed humans to build larger, stronger, and more durable structures.
qAndA.question: Why was the replacement of iron with steel so impactful?

scenes.title: Introduction

narrativeProgression.description: Copper is perfect for carrying electricity.

scenes.title: Copper and its Uses

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator explains that aluminum can also be made into alloys, which makes it stronger.

characterInteraction.description: Boy 1, Girl, and Boy 2 are shown standing next to a steel ring, seemingly observing it.
Cowboy, Man with asian hat, Man with a red fez, and Man with hat are shown in a line, representing the discovery of steel in different cultures at different times.

narrativeProgression.description: The narrator explains that steel is much stronger and can last far longer than previous materials used in construction.

scenes.thematicElements: The narrator discusses the historical impact of steel and explains why its strength and low cost have made it such a significant material in construction and industry.
scenes.title: Steel and Its Impact

scenes.thematicElements: The narrator summarizes the key properties and uses of metals discussed in the video.
scenes.title: Summary of Metal Uses

scenes.title: Credits and Licensing

climax.description: The narrator explains that the use of steel in industry and construction since the 19th century has changed the face of Earth.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: In this video, you're going to examine the uses of metals.
The periodic table of elements has 91 pure metals in it.
How many can you think of?
The properties of these metals are due to their atomic structure, as is their position
in the periodic table of elements.
This atomic structure also has a bearing on how the metals are used.
Consider some of the most unreactive metals you know of.
These metals may be gold or silver.
Think about how these metals are used.
They are valuable, perhaps more important in terms of their use, is that they are very
unreactive.
They do not react with air or water.
A ring or jewellery is often given as a special gift.
Because of its unreactive nature, the jewellery will remain shiny and untarnished.
Copper is also an unreactive metal.
Can you think of a use for copper?
Because it does not react with water being below hydrogen in the reactivity series.
Copper used to be used for the construction of water pipes.
You may have copper pipes carrying water around your home.
Copper is also malleable and can be bent easily without cracking,
so it can be made to bend around corners.
As well as its low reactivity, the ability of copper to conduct electricity is important.
When considering how it is used, copper is a good conductor of electricity and is ductime.
This means it can be drawn out into long wires.
Perfect for carrying electricity from place to place.
Aluminum is another metal that has been specifically used because of its characteristics.
Aluminum will react with oxygen in the air to form a layer of aluminium oxide.
This layer is relatively strong and can protect the main body of the metal.
The fact that the aluminium reacts in this way means that it can be used for the bodies of trains.
It does not need painting and its tarnish look is protective of the layers below.
Aluminum is also used for the bodies of plane.
Aluminum is less dense than many metals, making it light.
It can also be made stronger, making it into an alloy.
This aluminium alloy can be bent easily to form the body of the plane.
Steel is another metal which has changed the face of the earth and the way humans use the materials around them.
Steel is also strong, but perhaps more importantly it is cheap to make.
Iron, when combined with carbon, becomes the compound steel.
Iron by itself is a weak metal, but when carbon is added to form steel,
it becomes considerably stronger.
Iron has been in plentiful supply and used by humans for thousands of years.
Steel has been discovered by different cultures at different times in history,
but particularly the replacement of iron.
By steel, in industry and construction since the 19th century, changed the face of the earth.
It has allowed for the building of many large constructions, such as bridges.
Much stronger and able to last far longer than previous constructions.
So in summary, there are a wide variety of metals which humans have exploited for their varying properties.
Some metals are unreactive with water and air, making them useful for jewelry and piping.
Some metals are less dense than others, and therefore useful for the aerospace industry.
Some metals are good conductors of electricity.
